## Comment conventions

Comments are prefixed to signal intent:

- `blocking:` must be addressed before merge.
- `suggestion:` optional improvement; the author decides.
- `question:` the reviewer needs information, not a change.

# Testing Strategy

Owner: Developer Experience (DevEx)

## The test pyramid

We aim for roughly 70% unit tests, 20% integration tests and 10% end-to-end
tests by count. Unit tests run on every commit, integration tests run on every
pull request, and end-to-end tests run on merge to `main` and nightly against
staging.

## Unit tests

Unit tests exercise one module in isolation and run without network, disk or
clock dependencies. A unit test suite for a service MUST finish in under 60
seconds on a laptop. Tests that need the clock use the injected `Clock`
interface; tests that need randomness seed it explicitly.

Postmortems are blameless. They describe what the system and the people in it

## Template

The template in the `postmortems` repository has these sections:

## Burn-rate alerts

Each SLO has two alerts: a fast burn (2% of the monthly budget consumed in one

# Service Level Objectives and Error Budgets

Owner: Site Reliability Engineering (SRE)

## Definitions

- A **Service Level Indicator (SLI)** is a measurement: the fraction of
  requests that succeed, or the fraction that complete under a latency bound.
- A **Service Level Objective (SLO)** is a target for an SLI over a window, for
  example "99.9% of requests succeed over 30 days".
- An **error budget** is the allowed failure: 100% minus the SLO. At 99.9% over
  30 days the budget is about 43 minutes of full downtime.

- An **error budget** is the allowed failure: 100% minus the SLO. At 99.9% over
  30 days the budget is about 43 minutes of full downtime.

## Required SLOs

Every tier-1 and tier-2 service defines at least an availability SLO and a
latency SLO in its `service.yaml`. The defaults, which teams may tighten but
not loosen without SRE approval:

| Tier | Availability | Latency |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | 99.95% | p95 under 300 ms |
| 2 | 99.9% | p95 under 500 ms |
| 3 | 99.5% | p95 under 1000 ms |

SLOs are measured at the load balancer, not inside the service, so they
include the effects of deploys and infrastructure.

# Secrets Management

Owner: Security

## Where secrets live

All secrets live in HashiCorp Vault. Secrets are never stored in git, in
container images, in CI variables, in Slack, or in tickets. The
`secret-scanner` pre-receive hook rejects pushes containing strings that
match known credential patterns, and a weekly scan of the entire organisation
catches anything that slipped through.

## Paths

Vault paths follow `secret/<environment>/<service>/<name>`, for example
`secret/prod/order-router/db-password`. Shared secrets used by several
services live under `secret/<environment>/shared/` and are owned by Platform.

# Backups and Disaster Recovery

Owner: Data Platform

## Backup schedule

Every production Postgres cluster takes a full base backup daily at 02:00 UTC
and ships write-ahead logs continuously to object storage in a different
region. Point-in-time recovery is possible to any second within the last 35
days. Object storage buckets that hold customer files are versioned and
replicated cross-region with a 15-minute lag.

## Restore testing

A random production database is restored into an isolated environment every
week by the `restore-drill` job. The drill verifies that the restore
completes, that row counts match the source within the expected lag, and
that the application's smoke tests pass against the restored copy. A failed
drill pages the Data Platform on-call.

# Caching

Owner: Platform

## Layers

Larkspur caches at three layers, each with a different owner:

1. **Edge cache** - the CDN caches public, unauthenticated responses with
   `Cache-Control` headers set by the service. Owned by Web Platform.
2. **Application cache** - Redis clusters, one per team, used for sessions,
   rate-limit counters and computed results. Owned by the service team.
3. **In-process cache** - small LRU caches inside a service for configuration
   and reference data. Owned by the service team.

# Messaging and Events

Owner: Data Platform

## Platform

Asynchronous communication between services uses Kafka. There is one cluster
per production region with six brokers and a replication factor of three.
Topics are created through the `kafka-topic` Terraform module; ad-hoc topic
creation is disabled.

## Topic naming

Topics are named `<domain>.<entity>.<event>` in the past tense, for example
`orders.order.created` or `payments.refund.settled`. Topics are owned by the

# RFC Process

Owner: Architecture Review Board

## When to write an RFC

An RFC (Request for Comments) is required for any change that affects more
than one team, introduces a new datastore, language or framework, changes a
public API in a breaking way, or is expected to take more than six engineer
weeks. Smaller design decisions are captured as Architecture Decision Records
instead.

## Template

RFCs live in the `rfcs` repository as Markdown files named
`NNNN-short-title.md`. The template has these sections: **Summary**,
**Motivation**, **Proposal**, **Alternatives considered**, **Rollout and
migration**, **Security and privacy review**, **Open questions**.

An RFC SHOULD be readable in 15 minutes. Long appendices go in a linked
document.

# Architecture Decision Records

Owner: Architecture Review Board

## Purpose

An Architecture Decision Record (ADR) captures a single technical decision,
its context and its consequences, so that future engineers understand why
the system looks the way it does. ADRs are lightweight: one page, written by
the person making the decision, reviewed by the team.

## When to write one

Write an ADR when a decision is hard to reverse, when it will surprise
someone reading the code later, or when the team debated it for more than an
hour. Choosing a library, deciding how to model a core entity, or picking a
consistency model all qualify. Decisions that affect multiple teams need an
RFC instead.

Every repository commits its lockfile: `uv.lock` for Python,

## Canary analysis

Production deploys start with a canary that receives 5% of traffic for ten
minutes. The canary is promoted automatically when all of the following hold
compared with the baseline:

- HTTP 5xx rate is not more than 0.5 percentage points higher
- p95 latency is not more than 15% higher
- no new panic or unhandled-exception signature appears in logs

If any check fails, the canary is rolled back automatically and the pipeline
posts to the owning team's alerts channel.

Production services run at least three replicas. Horizontal Pod Autoscalers

# Kubernetes Platform

Owner: Platform

## Clusters

Larkspur runs four Kubernetes clusters on managed cloud Kubernetes: `dev`,
`staging`, `prod-eu` and `prod-us`. Production clusters run three control
plane replicas across availability zones. Cluster versions track the upstream
release minus one minor version and are upgraded quarterly.

## Workload requirements

Every deployment MUST declare:

- CPU and memory requests and limits. Memory limit equals memory request;
  CPU limit is at most four times the CPU request.
- A readiness probe and a liveness probe on distinct endpoints

- A `PodDisruptionBudget` allowing at most one unavailable replica.
- Pod anti-affinity across zones for tier-1 services.
- Resource labels: `app.kubernetes.io/name`, `larkspur.com/team`,
  `larkspur.com/tier`.

## Metrics

Metrics follow Prometheus naming: `larkspur_<service>_<name>_<unit>`, for
example `larkspur_order_router_requests_total`. Every HTTP and gRPC service
exposes the RED metrics (rate, errors, duration) automatically through the
telemetry middleware. Histograms use the shared bucket set
`[5ms, 10ms, 25ms, 50ms, 100ms, 250ms, 500ms, 1s, 2.5s, 5s, 10s]`.

Cardinality is the main risk: labels MUST NOT include user ids, order ids or
other unbounded values. The metrics pipeline drops any series whose label set
exceeds 10,000 distinct combinations and posts a warning.

# Observability

Owner: Site Reliability Engineering (SRE)

## The three signals

Every service emits structured logs, Prometheus metrics and OpenTelemetry
traces. The `larkspur-telemetry` library for each language configures all
three with a single initialisation call and injects the `trace_id` into logs.

## Logging

Logs are JSON lines written to stdout and shipped by the cluster's Vector
agent to Loki. Required fields are `timestamp`, `level`, `service`,
`trace_id` and `message`. Log levels are `DEBUG`, `INFO`, `WARN` and `ERROR`;
production runs at `INFO`. Logging request bodies or any personal data is
forbidden; the `log-scrubber` filter redacts known patterns (emails, card
numbers, bearer tokens) as a safety net, not as a substitute for care.

Log retention is 30 days in Loki, with `ERROR` lines additionally archived to
object storage for one year.

# Mobile Release Process

Owner: Mobile Platform

## Applications

Larkspur ships two mobile applications: the customer app (iOS and Android)
and the field-operations app (Android only). Both are built from the
`mobile` monorepo with React Native and Expo, with native modules in Swift
and Kotlin where required.

## Weekly train

The mobile train is cut every Tuesday at 10:00 UTC from `main`. The build is
distributed to internal testers through TestFlight and the Play internal
track within an hour. After a 24-hour soak, the release manager submits to
both stores on Wednesday. Store review typically completes within 24 hours
for iOS and a few hours for Android.

# Release Trains and Versioning

Owner: Release Engineering

## Cadence

Backend services deploy continuously: every merge to `main` that passes CI is
deployed to `staging` automatically and to production after the canary
analysis described in the deployment page. There is no fixed release day.

Mobile applications and the customer-facing web application ship on a weekly
release train. The train is cut every Tuesday at 10:00 UTC from `main`,
soaks on staging for 24 hours, and is released on Wednesday. Missing the train
means waiting for the next one; there are no "hold the train" requests except
for a declared incident.

# Messaging and Events

Owner: Data Platform

## Platform

Asynchronous communication between services uses Kafka. There is one cluster
per production region with six brokers and a replication factor of three.
Topics are created through the `kafka-topic` Terraform module; ad-hoc topic
creation is disabled.

## Topic naming

Topics are named `<domain>.<entity>.<event>` in the past tense, for example
`orders.order.created` or `payments.refund.settled`. Topics are owned by the
service that produces to them and have exactly one producer service.

The default TTLs are 15 minutes for computed results and 24 hours for
sessions. Values larger than 512 KB are rejected by the client library.

## Cache-aside pattern

Services use cache-aside: read from the cache, on a miss read from the
database and populate the cache. Write-through is used only for session
data. Services MUST function, albeit more slowly, when Redis is unavailable;
the client library returns a miss on connection errors and emits the
`cache_unavailable` metric.

## Idempotency

All `POST` endpoints that create resources accept an `Idempotency-Key`
header. Keys are stored for 24 hours; a repeated request with the same key
and body returns the original response, and a repeated key with a different
body returns HTTP 422.

## Rate limiting

Public APIs apply a per-key token bucket of 600 requests per minute with a
burst of 100. Responses include `RateLimit-Limit`, `RateLimit-Remaining` and
`RateLimit-Reset` headers, and a 429 response includes `Retry-After`.

# RFC Process

Owner: Architecture Review Board

## When to write an RFC

An RFC (Request for Comments) is required for any change that affects more
than one team, introduces a new datastore, language or framework, changes a
public API in a breaking way, or is expected to take more than six engineer
weeks. Smaller design decisions are captured as Architecture Decision Records
instead.

## Template

RFCs live in the `rfcs` repository as Markdown files named
`NNNN-short-title.md`. The template has these sections: **Summary**,
**Motivation**, **Proposal**, **Alternatives considered**, **Rollout and
migration**, **Security and privacy review**, **Open questions**.

An RFC SHOULD be readable in 15 minutes. Long appendices go in a linked
document.
